query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, degradation at elevated temperatures is governed by the synergistic segregation of key elements—particularly Cr and Ti—to the surface. Under oxidizing conditions, these elements form a continuous, adherent duplex oxide scale (with an inner Cr-rich layer and an outer Ti/Al-influenced layer) that slows further oxidation. Under reducing conditions, the insufficient oxidation results in discontinuous, porous oxide patches and favors internal oxidation, leading to more pronounced microstructural degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a stable fcc matrix
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to elevated temperatures (800–1000 °C) in controlled gas atmospheres—one oxygen-rich (oxidizing) and one hydrogen-rich (reducing)
generation.conditions: Temperature maintained between 800–1000 °C with identical sample processing (to avoid phase readjustment) under separately controlled oxidizing and reducing gas environments
generation.structural_mediator: Surface segregation and subsequent oxide scale formation involving Cr and Ti (with contributions from Al) that mediate the barrier properties of the scale
generation.mechanism: At high temperature in an oxidizing environment, Cr and Ti preferentially migrate to the surface to form stable oxides (Cr₂O₃, TiO₂) that develop into a continuous, adherent duplex oxide scale. This scale retards oxygen ingress and minimizes further degradation while the underlying fcc matrix remains intact. In contrast, under reducing conditions, limited oxide formation fails to create an effective barrier, thereby permitting internal oxidation and microstructural destabilization that accelerates degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: For samples exposed to oxidizing gases: formation of a thin, continuous, and duplex oxide scale with minimal subsurface damage. For samples under reducing conditions: formation of irregular, discontinuous or porous oxides accompanied by signs of internal oxidation and increased microstructural degradation relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with its intact fcc matrix before gas exposure
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for high-temperature exposures confined to 800–1000 °C where the fcc matrix is retained; if temperatures exceed this range or if gas compositions deviate substantially from the defined oxidizing/reducing conditions, different degradation phenomena may emerge.
generation.uncertainty: While the roles of Cr and Ti in forming protective oxides are supported by analogous studies in complex alloys, the precise kinetics of elemental segregation and the contributions of other elements (e.g., Co, Fe, Ni, Al) in the synergistic oxidation process require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of the additively manufactured alloy. Divide them into two groups: one group to be exposed to a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (O₂-rich) and the other to a reducing atmosphere (H₂-rich) at 800–1000 °C for fixed durations. After exposure, perform detailed surface and cross-sectional examinations using XPS, TEM, and SEM-EDS to analyze oxide scale thickness, continuity, composition, and any internal microstructural changes.
measurements: Thickness and uniformity of the oxide scale by TEM/SEM
Chemical composition profiles of the surface and subsurface layers via XPS/EDS
Evidence of internal oxidation or phase destabilization from cross-sectional analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under oxidizing conditions the alloy fails to develop a continuous, duplex oxide scale (or if the degradation levels are equivalent to or worse than those under reducing conditions), or if no significant differences in microstructural degradation between oxidizing and reducing environments are observed, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. In the case of Sn, the early research [,] concentrated on alloys where its concentration was low to avoid the formation of the A15-Nb3Sn compound. In 2007, Geng et al [] reported that the addition

The systematic change in the composition of the alloy and the calculation of the equilibrium diagrams using the Thermo-Calc software (Thermo-Calc Software AB, Solna, Sweden) [] and the TTNi7 database [] finally led to the alloy Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6, which has a wide temperature range of existence of a γ-γ’ two phase region and a high proportion of the ordered γ’ phase. The mechanical properties of this alloy are based on a stable microstructure in the temperature range up to 800 °C, as reported recently []. Temperature tensile strength and elongation to failure up to 800 °C [] are even superior to those of Alloy 800 and Inconel 617 []. At this temperature, Al10Co25Cr8Fe15Ni36Ti6 also has better mechanical properties than other high entropy alloys and compositionally complex alloys like solid solution Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 (~100 MPa, []) or equiatomic Al17Co17Cr17Cu17Fe17Ni17 (~180 MPa, []).

Considering that Hf, Si, Sn, and Ti are key elements for oxidation resistance and that refractory metals, in particular Mo and W, are key for strength and creep [,,,,], the synergy of Hf, Sn, and Ti that promotes Ti rich Nbss (i) improves the oxidation resistance of the Nbss but (ii) reduces the strength and creep of the Nbss in alloys with RM addition, owing to the relationship between the concentration of Ti and RMs in the Nbss in RM(Nb)ICs and RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs (e.g., see Figure S4 in the Supplemental Data in [], Figure 12 in [], and Figure 12 in []). Thus, a challenge for alloy design is to “balance” these effects. This is achievable with the alloy design methodology NICE [,,].

occupying_moves.technique: additive manufacturing under rigorously standardized parameters followed by controlled high‐temperature oxidation/reduction tests
occupying_moves.conditions: Maintain the baseline Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 composition and fcc phase by preventing phase readjustment during fabrication, then expose samples at 800–1000°C under separately controlled oxidizing (O₂-rich) and reducing (H₂-rich) atmospheres to decouple processing-induced variations from inherent material behavior

occupying_moves.technique: systematic oxidation testing combined with advanced surface and microstructural characterization (e.g., XPS, TEM, SEM-EDS)
occupying_moves.conditions: Use the baseline alloy that retains the fcc matrix and perform controlled incremental modifications—either by slight substitutions or by adjusting local elemental activities—while exposing specimens to elevated temperatures (800–1000°C) in alternately oxidizing and reducing gas environments; ensure that the mechanical integrity is not compromised by keeping within the compositional window established for strength and fatigue performance

chosen.technique: systematic high-temperature oxidation testing paired with advanced surface and microstructure characterization (e.g., XPS, TEM, SEM-EDS)
chosen.conditions: Expose the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy—designed to retain its fcc matrix—to temperatures between 800–1000°C under well-defined oxidizing (O₂-rich) versus reducing (H₂-rich) environments while implementing narrow, controlled compositional tweaks (or localized elemental activity adjustments) that preserve its mechanical integrity
chosen.why: This controlled comparison directly targets the unexplained synergistic elemental effects in oxidation degradation by isolating the impact of incremental changes under identical fcc conditions. It distinguishes the mechanistic hypothesis via standard high-entropy alloy oxidation experiments and advanced characterization, making it a plausible, testable intervention that builds directly on prior work while resolving a key limitation.
